chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad or someone else from Ibn Mahboub from Abdul Aziz al-Abdi from Abdullah ibn Abi Yafour who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever cultivates wheat in a land, and its produce does not become pure (or is not of good quality), or its produce comes out mostly as barley, this is due to the injustice of his work regarding the ownership of the land's surface, or due to injustice to his tenant farmers and lessees, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "So because of the injustice of those who were Jews, We forbade them the good things which had been lawful for them" — meaning the flesh of camels, cows, and sheep.'

And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, an Israelite, whenever he ate from the flesh of camels, would suffer pain in his lower back, so he forbade upon himself the flesh of camels, and that was before the Torah was revealed. So when the Torah was revealed, it did not forbid it, yet they did not eat it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual and practical reason for poor crop quality in Islamic jurisprudence according to the Imams?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates that agricultural decline or crop degradation often stems from the injustice (zulm) of landowners or tenants toward their workers, linking this to the Quranic principle that divine prohibitions can arise from human actions. He illustrates this with the example of an Israelite who self-forbade camel meat due to back pain before the Torah's revelation, continuing this practice even after the Torah did not forbid it, thereby showing how human custom can mimic divine law. This hadith highlights the Shia scholarly view on the interplay between social justice, agricultural productivity, and the flexibility of religious rulings based on context.
